To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the benefits that can be derived from Enterprise Systems in the Australian Public Service are substantial; (2) the barriers to the realization of these benefits are significant; and (3) there is a high degree of consensus amongst the stakeholders on the barriers to be removed.

the most significant barriers to benefits-realization in the public sector from enterprise systems are (i) lack of commitment from senior management, (ii) lack of commitment by vendors, (iii) lack of commitment and/or understanding of the need for change management, (iv) lack of commitment of the workforce to change, and (v) lack of understanding of the need to integrate systems and business processes.

the barriers to benefits-realization from Enterprise Systems in the public service are: the lack of an integrated approach to Enterprise Systems implementation and the lack of a common understanding of the role of Enterprise Systems in government.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of barriers to benefits from ES, and the development of a framework to support the management of those barriers.
the management of ES as a strategic investment in a public service context, where the benefits of such investments have been slow to materialise, and the risks of failure are high.

the management of large-scale software systems that are intended to provide integrated services across the enterprise, and that require a significant commitment to the re-engineering of business process and organisational structures.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there is a lack of evidence of the successful use of enterprise systems in the public service.

ES are not the panacea for all public sector ills, but that the benefits of ES are not being realised because of the lack of a shared vision of what they can do, and a lack of a shared understanding of the processes that are required to achieve this.
the barriers to benefits-realization from enterprise systems are not insurmountable, and the benefits of enterprise systems are not unattainable.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the ES experience is a complex and challenging one, and the research methodology developed to examine this experience has been found to be effective in identifying the barriers to benefits-realization.
the ES life cycle is a complex and dynamic process, and that it is not sufficient to consider only one aspect of the life cycle.

the barriers to benefits-realization from ES in the public service can be grouped into three categories: (1) the barriers that relate to the public service itself, (2) the barriers that result from the vendor's approach to the sale of the product and (3) the barriers that stem from the consultants who are involved in implementing the system.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there is a need for a more holistic approach to enterprise systems in public service.
the public sector has the potential to benefit from enterprise systems in ways that are not currently being exploited.
ES are a strategic technology that requires a strategic approach to implementation.
